back: **License determinations**, **restricted-party screening match decisions** and **voluntary disclosures**. The Senior is your checker and remains the owner of exports.
extra: A possible screening match is put on hold and escalated, never cleared by a hire. Filing decisions and anything with a regulatory deadline also stay with the Senior. Suitable items for you: data corrections, master-data fixes with review, report tweaks, documentation and reconciliations.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: What is a standard cost, and what is it compared with?
back: A **predetermined cost per item** (material, freight, duty, overhead) that values inventory and cost of goods sold until the next cost update. **Actual costs** are compared with it; the differences are variances such as PPV.
extra: Why a stale standard matters: when duty or freight changes and the standard does not, the difference lands in variance accounts instead of in item cost, and reported margins absorb it.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: What does landed cost add on top of the supplier's price?
back: Everything it takes to get the item into our warehouse: **international freight and insurance**, **duties and customs fees**, and **brokerage and inland freight**.
extra: Recoverable import taxes (Canada GST, Mexico IVA) are normally not a cost: confirm with Finance and never add them by default. Freight is allocated by a documented driver, such as weight, kept the same between cycles unless Finance agrees a change.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: KIT-300 (US import): FOB $40.00, ocean freight $3.00, insurance $0.20 per unit; hypothetical duty 5% ad valorem. What is the duty per unit?
back: **$2.00** = 5% × $40.00. US customs value excludes international freight and insurance identified separately, so the duty base is $40.00, not $43.20 or the $46.50 landed cost.
extra: Common mistake: rate × landed cost (5% × $46.50 = $2.325, about $2.33) overstates duty on every item from that lane. The cost cycle catches it with a hand check of items per import country against the duty base rules.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: PART-A sells for $20.00 with a $14.00 landed standard. A new hypothetical 10% duty applies to its $10.00 customs value. What happens to its margin?
back: Duty adds **$1.00** (10% × $10.00), so landed cost becomes $15.00. Gross margin falls from $6.00 (**30%**) to $5.00 (**25%**) unless the price changes.
extra: This is the Tariff-Impact Model's logic: only the duty changes, with freight, fees and prices held constant. Its new standard is an estimate for decisions; the Oracle load still goes through the full standard cost cycle.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: In a standard cost cycle, which two sign-offs must be in place before anything loads to Oracle?
back: The **checker's review** (the Manager; the Senior for duty-rate or classification questions) and **Finance's written approval** of the cost changes and the revaluation estimate. The maker never approves their own file.
extra: Why: a wrong standard instantly misstates inventory value and margins. The rule continues after day 90. The approved file is locked read-only; any later change is a new version with a new review and approval.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: In a standard cost cycle, what happens to the collected inputs at the end of Phase 2, before anything is calculated?
back: They are **frozen** (by default at T-15): the input pack is saved read-only with every extract's timestamp and linked on the Jira epic. Later changes wait for the next cycle unless Finance and the Manager approve.
extra: Why: the checker must review exactly what the cost file was built from. A change after the freeze breaks that link, and the loaded costs no longer match what was reviewed.
source: Standard cost update checklist, Phases 1 and 2

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::2 Standard and landed cost
front: During the first 90 days, who posts the standard cost update to Oracle production?
back: **Whoever posts it today** keeps doing it. Hire B prepares and checks the cost inputs as maker; an Oracle cost update is not a tool a hire can own.
extra: Any exception needs written approval from the Manager, the Finance controller and ERP security, covers only the cost-update function, and must pass the segregation-of-duties check. Maker-checker applies either way.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: What must you show at the day-60 review for the Manager to grant production change rights for your owned tool?
back: All six **'owns one tool'** points on the diagram, including **one end-to-end run**, a **tool doc** the Manager could follow alone, and **one change tested** in the test copy through a change request.
extra: Point 2 also means you can name the tool's known failure modes and how to recover from each. The rights then cover only that tool, and only through change control.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: For the day-60 'owns one tool' criteria, which end-to-end run of the tool counts?
back: One run is enough, **either** supervised in production with the current knowledge holder, who executes every production write, **or** alone on a test copy.
extra: Write the tool doc's run steps while you do them, with screenshots. Mark any step you did not perform yourself 'not yet verified'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: For day 60 you propose an e2open disposition for your owned tool. Which options can it take?
back: **Replace, interface, retire or keep**, or **TBD** with the open question written down. The disposition is confirmed after the e2open kickoff.
extra: Business rules hidden in the tool's code must not be lost in the migration: list them in the tool doc so they reach the requirements.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: Before day 60, you have changed and tested your owned tool in the test copy. Who puts the change into production?
back: **The Manager**, after the checker review and approval. Before the day-60 review you have no production write access, so you never deploy a change yourself.
extra: From the day-60 review, if the Manager grants change rights, you may implement changes to that one tool yourself, still only through a change request with a checker.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: Which test must every tool change request include, whatever the change?
back: A **regression test**: run the old and new versions on the same input and confirm that the only differences are the ones you intended.
extra: Example: a fix to keep HTS numbers as 10-digit text changed exactly the 312 truncated rows, only in the HTS column, and nothing else. Attach the comparison to the Jira issue.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: Who is the checker for changes to a tool you own, before and after day 60?
back: **The Manager**, always. Owning a tool never means approving your own change: the maker is never the checker.
extra: The checker reviews the code or configuration diff, the test evidence, the impact rows and the rollback plan, and records the decision on the Jira issue. No approval, no implementation.
source: Change request template (Who uses it; section 10)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: A tool change's first production run goes wrong. Which part of the change request, written before implementing, says what to do?
back: The **rollback plan**: the result that triggers it, who decides, the steps and the time they take, and where the verified backup is.
extra: Confirm the backup exists before you implement. With a written plan you restore the previous version in minutes instead of improvising. Plan the clean-up of any outputs the faulty version already sent to a broker or Finance.
source: Change request template, step 7 and section 8

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::3 Owning a tool
front: How is a tool change approved when the tool is sending wrong data to a broker right now?
back: As an **Emergency** change: the Manager's verbal go-ahead, a checker review the same day, and the change request template completed within 1 working day.
extra: Emergency is only for production producing wrong data now. If a workaround has already stopped the bad data, it is a Normal change: test fully first.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: A one-cell fix to a tool's HTS handling looks tiny. Which SDLC phases may it skip, and what does its size change?
back: **None.** A one-cell fix and an e2open release go through the same phases. Size decides only how much **paperwork**; the risk rating (Low, Medium, High) decides how much **testing and approval**.
extra: Tiny changes to HTS or rate handling are where the worst errors start. For a small tool change, a Jira story covers intake and requirements, the change request covers design through release, and the tool doc's change history closes it.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: When does testing happen in waterfall, and how does the V-model change that?
back: **Waterfall:** only after all development, so a misunderstood requirement surfaces last, when it is most expensive to fix. **V-model:** each development phase is paired with a test level, and each test is written with its requirement or design.
extra: Business requirements pair with acceptance testing; UAT is one form of it, done by the intended users. Our tool changes run like a small V-model: acceptance criteria first, build in a copy, test at each level, release through a change request.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: In Scrum, which commitment goes with the Increment, and what happens to work that does not meet it?
back: The **Definition of Done**. Work that does not meet it cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review. The team's definition of done for Jira issues plays the same role.
extra: Scrum basics (2020 Scrum Guide): one team with three accountabilities, Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, and Sprints of one month or less. The Product Backlog's commitment is the Product Goal; the Sprint Backlog's is the Sprint Goal.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: Boundary test of the Duty Rate Lookup's as-of date: which of PART-A's rate rows should it list as of 2026-12-31, and as of 2027-01-01?
back: **2026-12-31: 2 rows**, Base and Action X-0 on its last day. **2027-01-01: 1 row**, Base only. A query that keeps a row only when To is **after** the as-of date, not **on or after** it, wrongly drops X-0 on 2026-12-31.
extra: To is the last day the rate applies, so a row stays in while To is on or after the as-of date. Test both sides of every start and end date, as T1 to T3 in the primer's Part 10 do: a happy-path test misses off-by-one errors.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: Before a tool change may leave test for production, which three gates must it pass, in order?
back:
1. **Tests run**, with the evidence saved.
2. **Checker review** of the diff, the evidence and the rollback plan.
3. **Approval** by the Manager, on the Jira issue.
Only then is it released.
extra: For a system the team does not own, its system owner approves too. Even a Standard (pre-authorized) change keeps maker-checker every time. The release checklist also needs no open Critical or High defects, a verified backup and users told.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: At release, what must the version that goes to production be, and what may differ from the test copy?
back: **Exactly the tested version**: the same file, tag or solution version. Only the environment settings switch to production values, such as paths, connections and environment variables.
extra: A change can pass in test and still fail in production because it runs under another account: in test you use your personal login; in production a job, gateway data source or flow connection may run as the service account. Note each connection's account per environment.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: After a tool release, which step must pass before the change request is closed, and what is your part in it before day 60?
back: The **post-release check**: the first output matches the expected result, its counts tie to the input, and the production connection and account work. Before day 60 you do only its **read-only parts**.
extra: It opens with a smoke test: a quick check that the main functions work. The Manager or the knowledge holder does every production step before the day-60 review. Receivers confirm, the tool doc and SOP are updated, and the CR closes with evidence.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: A post-release check finds a wrong output, and the cause looks easy to fix. What comes first, and what must nobody do?
back: **Roll back first, investigate second**: restore the previous version from the verified backup, as the rollback plan says. **Never debug in production.**
extra: Restoring the old version does not recall what the faulty one already sent, such as a broker file or a cost input: the rollback plan must also say how those outputs are found and corrected. Where rollback is impossible, release only with a tested fix-forward ready.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 05 · Weeks 5–6 · Exports, standard and landed cost, owning a tool, SDLC::4 SDLC and change delivery
front: The broker file did not arrive this morning; it fails whenever the extract runs late. Which is the incident, and which the problem?
back: **Incident:** today's missing file; restore service and limit the damage. **Problem:** why it keeps failing (the late extract); find and remove the cause. Moving the job after the extract is the **change**.
extra: ITIL 4: an incident is an unplanned interruption to a service or reduction in its quality; a problem is a cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents. Log both as Jira bugs; the fix goes through a change request. Before day 60, never pause, re-run or fix production yourself.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: A new Canadian surtax: which document has legal effect, and which tells you how to declare it in CARM?
back: The **Order in Council** under the Customs Tariff (registered as an SOR) has legal effect. The **CBSA Customs Notice** says how CBSA applies it, including the surtax code to declare. If they differ, the order governs.
extra: Relief comes through a separate remission order (Customs Tariff section 115) with its own CBSA notice. Remission is claimed, not automatic, and is often extended in pieces.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: A Canadian surtax order has been made. Where is its official text published, and when does it take effect?
back: In the **Canada Gazette, Part II**, with its Regulatory Impact Analysis Statement. It takes effect under its own coming-into-force provision, which can be before publication.
extra: Gazette Part I carries proposals and consultations, not orders. Regular Part II issues come every second Wednesday; urgent orders can appear in special issues. Check for errata.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: A Mexican decree changes TIGIE rates. Where is it legally published, and where do you find its entry-into-force date?
back: In the **DOF** (Diario Oficial de la Federación). Entry into force is set in its **transitory articles**, often the day after publication.
extra: Check the evening (vespertina) and extraordinary editions too, not only the morning one. SAT and ANAM then say how to file the pedimento, and validation changes can lag the legal date.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: A colleague in Pricing asks you: 'How much will this tariff cost us?' What is the Research answer?
back:
"Standard Cost will model it from brief v1.0. I can tell you which items, from when and at what rate."
You never estimate the $ yourself.
extra: Never put $ figures, pricing advice or shipment-timing advice in a brief. Any $ figure is a material error in the trainer's review rubric, and the brief is sent back.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: Your daily scan finds an action that may touch our items, effective in 12 business days. Whom do you tell, when, and with what?
back: **The Manager and the Senior, the same day**, with the effective date and your first candidate count. Escalate any possible hit that takes effect within 15 business days.
extra: At 12 business days the urgency rule makes you maker, and the checker reviews your draft on the same business day you submit it. Below 5 business days, a trainer is maker.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: Scoping items for a country-specific action, which country do you match on, and which must you never use?
back: The **country of origin in our classification master**, never the supplier's or the ship-from country. Flag every item where those differ. Origin taken from the supplier address is a material error.
extra: Also check which origin rule the action itself uses: normal non-preferential origin, or its own rule, such as melt-and-pour for steel or smelt-and-cast for aluminum.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::1 Research track
front: Brief v1.0 is released. What happens in the 15-minute handoff call, and when is the handoff complete?
back: Hire A walks Hire B through the **scope, the dates and the open questions**, including any partial-value base. It is complete when Hire B confirms on the Jira story that the inputs are understood.
extra: Any change after release is a new version (v1.1), re-checked and re-sent to Standard Cost. The model's Action tab names the brief version it was built from.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: KIT-400's standard is $14.00. Receipts: 500 units at $14.60 actual, then 300 at $13.80. What is the total PPV?
extra: Common mistake: averaging the two prices without weighting by quantity (gives +160.00). PPV % = PPV ÷ standard value received: 240 ÷ (14.00 × 800) = 2.1%.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: KIT-400 shows a large unfavorable PPV this month. Which three kinds of driver do you check before you explain it to Finance?
back: **Price** (supplier price or FX), **landed-cost changes** (freight, or duty such as a new tariff action) and a **wrong standard** (stale, mis-keyed or in the wrong unit of measure).
extra: Report outliers separately and never delete them: in the practice pack, an actual cost above 3 times standard or below a third of it. Confirm Finance's PPV sign convention before you explain the number.
source: Analytics practice pack, Exercise 5; Standard cost checklist, Phase 4

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: Duty paid on KIT-400 differs from the duty in its standard cost. Which variance shows the difference?
back: **It depends on the company setting.** Duty brought in through landed-cost charges on the receipt shows in **PPV**. Duty absorbed at standard as a material overhead shows as **duty absorption versus actual**.
extra: Know which before you explain a variance to Finance. Until the standard is updated, a new tariff lands in that variance, and reported margins absorb it.
source: Standard cost checklist, Company settings and Phase 7

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: In Oracle EBS, why must the pending cost type hold each item's complete cost, not only the changed duty?
back: The update **replaces the item's whole Frozen cost** with its pending cost. A duty-only file would wipe the other cost elements, so copy the current Frozen costs in first, then apply the changes.
extra: The Phase 6 complete-cost check and the simulation catch it: look for large negative revaluations.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: You disagree with the brief's stacking reading for three items. What do you do instead of changing the model?
back: **Comment on the Research story** with the items and your reason. Hire A decides and, if needed, corrects the Action tab and re-releases the brief. You never edit Action, and never work around it on Items.
extra: Research decides scope, rates, duty base and stacking; Standard Cost computes the $ on those determinations. Workarounds that break the boundary rule: blanking an origin, or changing an HTS, to push an item out of scope.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::2 Standard Cost track
front: On the model's Items tab, KIT-400's customs value is per box of 12 but its standard cost is per each. What goes wrong?
back: The duty change is **multiplied by the pack size**, so it comes out 12 times too big. Customs value, quantity, standard cost and sell price must all be per the Oracle primary unit of measure.
extra: Convert before you paste and record the conversion in column N. The usual warning sign is the NOTE 'customs value above standard cost'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: In the shared Tariff-Impact Model, which tab does each track fill, and from what?
back: **Research** fills the **Action tab** from the checked brief: scope, rates, dates, duty base, stacking. **Standard Cost** fills the **Items tab** from the item extract. Neither edits the other's tab.
extra: Calc and Summary are formulas only. The checker logs every review on the Review tab and on Jira: the Senior checks the Action tab, the Manager checks the $ and approves release.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: For a duty on part of the value, which model tab holds each item's dutiable share, and who enters it?
back: The **Items tab** (column M), entered by **Standard Cost** from the source Research names in Brief Part 7. Research sets the duty base to PART; the checker traces the shares.
extra: Research states the base; Standard Cost does the arithmetic. A PART item with no share is a CHECK, and so is a share entered on an item whose rate taxes the full value.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: PART-A: $200.00 value, pays 2.5% base + 10% Action Y. A new 25% duty arrives. Duty per unit if it adds? If it displaces Y?
extra: In the model, enter a displaced duty per rate line (column AF) or per item (determinations column S). It must already be inside the item's current rate on Items, or Calc shows a CHECK.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: PART-A ($200.00) pays 2.5% base + 10% Action Y. Y rises to 20%. ADD or REPLACE, and what is the new duty per unit?
back: **REPLACE**, with an earlier rate of 10%: 12.5% + 20% − 10% = 22.5%, so **$45.00** per unit, up $20.00. ADD would wrongly give 32.5% ($65.00).
extra: In the model: Action B16 = REPLACE and B17 = 10%. With REPLACE, the current rate on Items must already include the earlier 10%, or Calc shows a CHECK.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: A new additional duty's text says nothing about other duties on the same goods. How does it combine with them?
back: It **adds** to the base rate and to each other duty: that is the default. Non-stacking needs a 'does not apply to' or interaction paragraph in the instrument itself.
extra: Read every instrument's interaction text and CBP's reporting-order guidance (research checklist step 9). Traps: double-counting, and assuming non-stacking without a text. The checker confirms the stacking result for at least 3 items that carry other duties.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: PUMP-50 qualifies for USMCA: customs value $500.00, non-US content 40%. A 25% duty applies to non-US content only. Duty per unit?
back: **$50.00**: 500.00 × 40% = 200.00 duty base, then 200.00 × 25% = 50.00. That is 10% of the full value. Charging it on the full $500.00 would give $125.00.
extra: This is USMCA treatment PARTIAL: the item stays in scope and gets relief through a rate line for USMCA-qualifying goods with a PART base. The reverse is also a material error: a content base where the action taxes the full value.
source: Tariff-Impact Model guide, Duty base and partial USMCA relief

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::3 Tariff mechanics
front: What decides whether USMCA-qualifying goods escape a new US additional duty, and what are the possible outcomes?
back: **Only the action's own text.** It may exempt them, give partial relief (a lower rate, or duty on the non-US content only), or give no relief at all.
extra: 'Made in Mexico' is not 'USMCA-qualifying'. Some carve-outs cover only goods 'entered free of duty under USMCA', so the claim must be on the entry line and the certification current.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::4 Data mapping and UAT
front: When do you write a UAT test case's expected result, and how exact must it be?
back: **Before you run it, with exact values**, for example 'Duty $2,750.00'. Work duty out with the Tariff-Impact Model or by hand. 'Works correctly' is not an expected result.
extra: The checker reviews the cases before execution: that review is an entry criterion. Record actual results in words and values too, even on a pass.
source: UAT test plan template, How to fill this in

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::4 Data mapping and UAT
front: After a defect found in UAT is fixed, what must you run besides the test case that failed?
back: **Regression**: re-run the related cases to prove that what worked before still works, after retesting the failed case itself.
extra: Example: after a fix for a rate chosen by PO date instead of entry date, retest that case and re-run the landed-cost case as regression. Log every defect the same day and link it to its case.
source: UAT test plan template, How to fill this in

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::4 Data mapping and UAT
front: Which open defects block the UAT exit criteria, and what do the remaining open ones need?
back: Any open **Critical or High** defect blocks exit. Each open Medium or Low defect needs a workaround, an owner and a fix date agreed by the business owner.
extra: The other exit criteria: 100% of Must cases executed and the target pass rate met, final data reconciliation passed, interface regression passed, evidence saved, sign-off recorded. The business owner then decides go or no-go.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::4 Data mapping and UAT
front: Profiling an AS400 extract, you find US HTS numbers with 9 digits. What happened, and how is it fixed?
back: A **leading zero was lost** (chapters 01–09) because the HTS was stored or opened as a number. Pad to 10 digits in the transform, fix the source too, and keep HTS as text.
extra: Opening an extract in Excel drops leading zeros and turns long numbers into scientific notation: load it into SQL, or import the CSV with those columns set to Text. Check HTS length by country in every profiling run.
source: Data mapping spec template, Parts 5 and 6

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::4 Data mapping and UAT
front: Profiling finds a code value that has no row in the mapping spec's value cross-reference. How do you treat it?
back: **As an open question** until it is mapped. List every distinct source value found in profiling, blanks and oddities included, and map each one to a target value or reject it explicitly.
extra: Example: one AS400 USMCA Y/N flag cannot move as is, because each country codes the claim differently: US SPI 'S' or 'S+', a Canadian tariff treatment code (10 or 11), and the Mexican pedimento coding.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: What makes a number you track a KPI rather than just a metric?
back: A **metric** is any number you track. A **KPI** is a metric tied to an objective, with a **target, an owner and a time frame**, and someone acts when it moves.
extra: Doran's original SMART (1981) had Assignable where later versions say Achievable: a KPI without an owner is just a metric. Most KPI arguments are about the definition (which items, which dates, open items), so write it first and compute second.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: What is the difference between a leading and a lagging KPI? Give a Research example of each.
back: A **lagging** KPI reports a result that has already happened: Research items released on time. A **leading** KPI warns before the result moves: the share of in-scope items with a confirmed HTS before an action takes effect.
extra: A good set has both: the lagging KPI confirms the result, the leading one lets you act in time. Standard Cost examples: PPV % is lagging; the share of standard value received within 5% of standard is leading.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: Designing a star schema in Kimball's four steps, what do you do right after choosing the business process, and why then?
back: **Declare the grain**: what one fact row means, in business words, such as one entry line as filed. Dimensions and facts come next, because each one must be true at that grain.
extra: Kimball calls not declaring the grain first the most frequent design error. The order: business process, grain, dimensions, facts. Write the grain down before you build anything.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: DimDate has one row per date for all of 2026. What must you still do to it before Duty Prior Month can use DATEADD?
back: **Mark it as the date table**, on its Date column. Power BI then checks it: unique dates, no blanks, no gaps. Classic time intelligence such as DATEADD needs a marked date table.
extra: Build it in DAX with CALENDAR(DATE(2026, 1, 1), DATE(2026, 12, 31)), so it spans full years, and sort Month name by Month number. Turn auto date/time off too, or Power BI adds a hidden date table for every date column.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: Some entry lines carry an item_id that is not in the item master. In the star model, which item row do they join to?
back: A **'Not in item master' row** added to DimItem for each such item_id, with UNK for chapter, origin and supplier country. Every fact row then finds its item, and no slicer shows (Blank).
extra: Kimball's rule: give a missing dimension value its own 'unknown' row instead of leaving the key unmatched. The row labels the gap but does not fix it: still count and report the orphan item IDs so the item master can be corrected.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: A card shows CALCULATE([Total Duty], DimItem[country_of_origin] = "X"). A slicer on that column is set to Y. What does the card show?
back: **Country X's duty.** CALCULATE evaluates an expression in a modified filter context: it adds, replaces or removes filters. Its filter on country_of_origin **replaces** the slicer's filter on that column, unless wrapped in KEEPFILTERS.
extra: Slicers on other columns, such as month, still apply. With KEEPFILTERS the two filters intersect, so the card goes blank. CALCULATE also turns row context into filter context.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: Duty MoM % divides by Duty Prior Month, which can be blank. What do DIVIDE and the / operator each return when it is?
back: **DIVIDE returns BLANK**, or the alternate result you give it: DIVIDE(5, 0, 1) returns 1. **The / operator returns Infinity or NaN**, which shows on the visual.
extra: Use DIVIDE whenever the denominator is an expression that can be zero or blank, such as a prior period or a total value; / is fine for a constant. BLANK is usually the best result: visuals drop groups whose measure is BLANK.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: PART-A duty: $8,000 in Q1 ($200,000 at 4.0%), $15,000 in Q3 ($250,000 at 6.0%). By Exercise 11's convention, what are the rate and value effects?
extra: Value the rate change at current value and the value change at base rate, and the two add up exactly. Using Q1 value and Q1 rate for both leaves $1,000 unexplained (2.0 pts × $50,000). Positive = more duty (unfavorable). Other conventions split the total differently, so name yours.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 06 · Weeks 7–9 · Track deep dives, tariff mechanics, data mapping, analytics depth::5 Analytics depth: models, measures, KPIs
front: Receipt cost ratios (actual ÷ standard) have quartiles Q1 = 0.95 and Q3 = 1.05. Which ratios does the 1.5 × IQR rule flag?
back: IQR = 1.05 − 0.95 = 0.10, so flag ratios **below 0.80 or above 1.20** (Q1 − 1.5 × IQR, Q3 + 1.5 × IQR). A flag means unusual, not wrong: **investigate it; never delete it.**
extra: Correct or remove a value only when it is shown to be in error (NIST). Many unusual cost lines are real price changes, exactly what a standard cost update needs. The z-score rule flags |z| > 3, with z = (ratio − mean) ÷ sample SD.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: What is US duty drawback, and what share of the eligible duties can it refund at most?
back: A refund of duties, taxes and fees paid on imports when the goods, a permitted substitute, or an article made from them is **exported or destroyed**. At most **99%**.
extra: The other 1% is not refunded. Antidumping and countervailing duties are never refunded at all (19 U.S.C. 1677h). TFTEA (2015) modernized drawback; current claims follow 19 CFR Part 190.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Which two questions place a US drawback claim in one of the five main types?
back:
1. **What happened** to the goods: used to make an export, exported or destroyed unused, or rejected.
2. Are the exported goods **the imported ones** (direct identification) or a **substitute**?
extra: Pre-TFTEA claims used 'same kind and quality' or 'commercially interchangeable'. Current claims use the 8-digit HTSUS tests. Drawback stays with the Senior: you only need to recognize which type a claim uses.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Unused substitution drawback, 1313(j)(2): when must the substitute match at 10 digits, and when is substitution unavailable?
back: When the 8-digit description begins with '**Other**', match at **10 digits**. If the 10-digit description also begins with 'Other', substitution is **not available**; direct identification still is.
extra: Common mistake: applying this 'Other' rule to 1313(b) manufacturing substitution. It belongs to 1313(j)(2) only. It is one reason item data must keep the full 10-digit HTS number.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Manufacturing substitution drawback, 1313(b): how closely must the substitute match the imported input?
back: **Same 8-digit HTSUS subheading**, and it may be imported or domestic. There is **no 10-digit 'Other' rule**: that rule applies only to unused substitution, 1313(j)(2).
extra: The substitute must also be used in manufacture within 5 years of the import it is designated against (19 CFR 190.22).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: PART-A: 1,000 units imported, $8,000.00 duty plus $2,000.00 antidumping duty; 600 exported unused. What is the maximum drawback?
back: **$4,752.00.** Eligible duty = 600 × ($8,000.00 ÷ 1,000) = $4,800.00. Refund = 99% × $4,800.00. The antidumping duty is never refunded by drawback.
extra: The 400 units that stayed in the US keep their duty paid. Common mistakes: refunding 100%, or including the antidumping duty, which would give $5,940.00.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Imported on 2026-03-10, PART-A is later exported unused. By what date must its drawback claim be filed?
back: **By 2031-03-10**: no later than 5 years after the date of importation (19 U.S.C. 1313(r)). The export or destruction must also fall within the 5-year window for its type.
extra: The clock runs from the import, not from the export. Old import entries drop out of the claim window, so drawback needs import data kept with dates.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: How long must the records behind a US drawback claim be kept, and why is that longer than it sounds?
back: Until **3 years after the drawback claim liquidates** (19 CFR 190.15), not 3 years after payment. Liquidation of the claim comes after any accelerated payment, so the clock starts late.
extra: Common mistake: applying the general 5 years from entry (19 CFR 163.4). Drawback records are usually kept longer, so a data migration must not archive or drop them early.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Which three kinds of records does a US drawback claim rely on?
back:
1. **Import** data: entries, lines, duty paid.
2. **Export** data: proof of export or destruction.
3. The **link** between them: inventory or manufacturing records.
extra: Why it matters to you: if your e2open data map drops entry-line detail or duty paid, a drawback claim loses its import support. Your drawback note lists what our records must keep.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: Who owns US duty drawback, and what is your drawback output by day 90?
back: **The Senior** keeps drawback. You attend the W11 overview and the W12 shadow, then write a 1-page note, '**what data drawback needs from our import and export records**'. It feeds your e2open data map.
extra: It is Stretch work (A90-9, B90-9). If the Senior is out in W11, the overview and the shadow both move to days 91–120.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::1 US duty drawback
front: PART-A was imported duty-paid into the US and later exported to Canada. How does USMCA limit its drawback?
back: To the **lesser of** the US duties paid and the duties paid when the goods enter **Canada** or Mexico (19 CFR 182.44). Goods listed in 182.45, such as originating goods, are exempt from this limit.
extra: Why it matters: CBP liquidates such a claim only once the duty paid in Canada or Mexico is established (19 CFR 182.50), so the claim needs that country's proof, such as the Mexican pedimento. The limit comes from USMCA Article 2.5.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: Which two e2open deliverables for your own process are your day-90 evidence, and in which migration phases are they made?
back: The **as-is process doc** (phase 1) and the **data map** with its data-quality log (phase 3). Draft them in W10–W11 and finalize them in W13.
extra: Both are Must criteria (A90-2, A90-3; B90-2, B90-3) and never give. They do not depend on the kickoff date: if the kickoff moves, bring whatever stage your drafts are at. W10 and W11 run at about half capacity, so start early.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: Designing the to-be process for e2open, what is the classic mistake, and what do you do instead?
back: **Rebuilding the AS400 inside e2open.** Instead, compare the process with e2open's standard (**fit-gap**) and record each real gap as a requirement.
extra: The to-be deliverable is the to-be steps, a gap list and requirements (requirements template). Map the as-is first: it is the baseline the gaps are measured against.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: You are mapping a source field to e2open but have no e2open data dictionary yet. What do you write as the target?
back: The **e2open concept**, marked '**target field TBC**'. Never guess a target field name: real names come only from the project's data dictionary or load templates.
extra: Guessing target names is the classic data-mapping pitfall. Write one row per target field, so unmapped target fields stay visible, and log each open question with an owner.
source: Data mapping spec template, How to fill this in

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: Profiling finds bad source data before the e2open load. Where is it fixed by default, and who decides?
back: **At the source**, on the **data owner's** decision. That keeps the AS400, the broker feeds and e2open in agreement during any parallel run. Fix in the transform only for mechanical rules such as zero-padding.
extra: 'Accept' needs the data owner's written reason; 'Exclude' needs their approval and an archive plan. A fix to classification, value or origin data is a compliance change: Research maker, Senior checker, change request.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: Before e2open cutover, who signs off UAT, and what must the parallel run show?
back: The **business owner** signs off UAT (go or no-go). The parallel run shows that AS400 and e2open outputs are **equal, or every difference is explained** by an approved change or a cleansing-log entry.
extra: Agree the comparisons and tolerances before the parallel run starts, and budget time for it. The common pitfalls are no time and no tolerance agreed in advance.
source: Trade systems primer §6.1; UAT test plan template §5 and §7

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: After each e2open test load, which three checks show the data arrived intact, and when does a check fail?
back: **Record counts** (total, by country, distinct keys), **control totals** (sums, or an HTS hash total) and **sample checks** (25 random plus all edge cases). Any unexplained difference fails the check.
extra: Only amount totals may have an agreed tolerance; counts and samples have none. Re-run every check after each test load and at cutover, and keep the queries, results, date and load ID together: they are UAT and audit evidence.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::2 e2open migration
front: Test load 1: AS400 has 41,250 records, e2open 41,232; 18 were excluded with approval. 39 of 40 sample rows match. What is the result?
back: **It fails.** The counts pass: 41,250 − 41,232 = 18, all explained by the approved exclusion. But the sample tolerance is **0**, so 1 mismatch fails the load. Fix the conversion, reload, re-run every check.
extra: Here a 1990s date loaded as 2090s. AS400 dates are often CYYMMDD: C = 0 for the 1900s, 1 for the 2000s (1261019 is 2026-10-19). Misread C and a date jumps a century.
source: Data mapping spec template, Filled example

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: What reporting work do you pick up in W10–W13, and who is your checker?
back: **One low-risk backlog item** the Senior picked in W9, such as a Power BI fix, a new measure or a warehouse view change. You are maker, **the Senior is checker**, and you demo it in W13.
extra: Start it only when your exports item 2 is done: one transition item at a time, and no more than 3 active Jira items in all.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: Days 60–90 overload you. What happens to your reporting item, and to your day-90 outcome?
back: Reporting is the **first transition work to give**: it slips past day 90 (Stretch, A90-8 and B90-8), and the **day-90 outcome does not change**.
extra: Trigger rule: if your as-is draft is under 50% at the end of W10, the reporting item pauses. Maker-checker, your cycle evidence, the as-is doc and the data map never give.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: A Power BI total differs from your SQL total. In what order do you look for the cause?
back:
1. The **filters** in force: slicers; visual, page or report filters.
2. The **relationships**: direction, inactive or unmatched keys.
3. The **measure** definition: sum vs average, exclusions.
extra: Same measure, different filter context, different value: that is why filters come first. Knowing why a total can differ from SQL is the base for every report change you make.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: A Power BI slicer shows '(Blank)'. What does it usually mean, and what do you do about it?
back: Some **fact rows have a key with no match in the dimension**, such as an entry line whose item is missing from the item table. Totals include them, so **fix the data**; don't hide the blank.
extra: Those rows are orphans. Joining them away in Power Query (an inner merge) makes the blank vanish but silently drops their amounts from the totals.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: Before you demo a changed Power BI report, how do you show that its numbers are right?
back: **Tie it out**: with no slicers, each card equals an independent SQL or Excel result. Then filter one value, such as one origin, and recheck it against SQL with the same filter.
extra: Record a tie-out table: measure, Power BI value, SQL or Excel value, difference. It is your evidence for the Senior's checker review.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Unit 07 · Weeks 10–13 · Drawback, e2open migration, reporting::3 Reporting
front: Your reporting backlog item is done. When do you write its closeout, and when may the epic be closed?
back: Within **5 working days** after the last child issue is Done (for a tool or system change, after go-live and the first clean production cycle). Close the epic only **after sign-off**.
extra: Every open item gets one owner, a date and a Jira key: no 'TBD' owners. Lessons learned are Keep, Stop and Start, each backed by a fact, with at most 3 actions.
source: Project closeout template, How to fill this in

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: Who can act as importer of record (IOR) on a US entry?
back: The owner or purchaser of the goods, or a licensed customs broker designated by the owner, purchaser or consignee (19 U.S.C. 1484).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is CBP's role in US imports?
back: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (part of DHS) releases goods, assesses and collects duties, taxes and fees, enforces trade laws, fixes final classification and value at liquidation, and operates ACE.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 2

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the CBSA's role in Canadian imports?
back: The Canada Border Services Agency releases imported goods, assesses and collects duties and taxes (including GST) through CARM, enforces border and trade laws, and licenses customs brokers.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 2

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How do ANAM and SAT divide responsibilities for Mexican imports?
back: ANAM (Agencia Nacional de Aduanas de México, operating since 1 Jan 2022 under SHCP) runs customs and collects foreign-trade duties. SAT remains the tax authority: RFC, e.firma, padrón de importadores and domestic taxes.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is an agente aduanal?
back: A Mexican customs broker: an individual holding a government-issued patente who prepares and files pedimentos and clears goods on the importer's behalf. Broker firms are called agencias aduanales.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does US entry type 01 mean?
back: Consumption entry, free and dutiable: the standard formal entry for commercial goods entering US commerce.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does US entry type 11 mean?
back: Informal entry, free and dutiable: a simplified entry for low-value shipments, generally US$2,500 or less (19 CFR 143.21). Quota and AD/CVD goods need formal entry; Chapter 99 goods have a separate, lower limit (as of Oct 2026)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: Under 19 CFR 143.21(a), what informal-entry limit applies to goods classified in HTSUS Chapter 99, Subchapters III and IV?
back: US$250, not the general US$2,500. Additional duties such as Sections 232 and 301 are reported in Chapter 99, so most tariffed shipments over US$250 need formal entry, as CBP confirmed in March 2025 (as of Oct 2026)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is ACE?
back: The Automated Commercial Environment: CBP's single-window system for processing US imports and exports. Brokers file entries into it, and importers can run reports on their own entries in the ACE Portal.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is ABI?
back: The Automated Broker Interface: the electronic (EDI) channel that brokers and self-filing importers use to transmit entries and entry summaries into ACE, built to CBP's CATAIR specifications.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: When do most US entries liquidate in practice?
back: About 314 days after the date of entry: ACE schedules automatic liquidation then unless liquidation is extended or suspended. Check the actual scheduled date in ACE (as of Oct 2026)
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 4.2

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the statutory deadline for CBP to liquidate a US entry?
back: One year from the date of entry (19 U.S.C. 1504), extendable to a maximum of four years. If CBP misses it, the entry is deemed liquidated at the rate, value and amount the importer declared.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is a Post-Summary Correction (PSC)?
back: An electronic correction to an accepted, unliquidated entry summary, filed through ACE, e.g., to fix classification, value or a preference claim. It can increase or decrease the duty owed.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does reasonable care require of a US importer?
back: A legal duty (19 U.S.C. 1484, from the 1993 Mod Act) to use care in entering, classifying and valuing goods and giving CBP accurate information. Relying on a broker does not transfer this duty.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is a US customs bond?
back: A surety contract guaranteeing CBP that duties, taxes and fees will be paid and entry obligations met. A single transaction bond covers one entry; a continuous bond covers all entries for a year and renews.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is ISF '10+2'?
back: Importer Security Filing for US-bound ocean cargo: the importer files 10 data elements (e.g., seller, buyer, manufacturer, country of origin, HTS-6) at least 24 hours before lading abroad; the carrier files 2 (stow plan, container status messages).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How long must US import records be kept?
back: Generally five years from the date of entry (19 CFR 163.4). More specific rules control where they exist; e.g., drawback records are kept until 3 years after the drawback claim is liquidated (19 CFR 190.15).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How long must Canadian import records be kept?
back: Six years following the importation of commercial goods, normally at the importer's place of business in Canada (Imported Goods Records Regulations; CBSA Memorandum D17-1-21).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How long must Mexican import records generally be kept?
back: Generally five years: the Código Fiscal de la Federación (art. 30) sets five years and defers to customs law for import documents. Program-specific rules (e.g., IMMEX) can differ; the Senior confirms them.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 3.4

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the primary customs valuation method in the US, Canada and Mexico?
back: Transaction value: the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the importing country, plus specified additions. All three follow the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What are the five statutory additions to US transaction value?
back: If not already in the price: packing costs, selling commissions paid by the buyer, assists, royalties or license fees paid as a condition of sale, and resale proceeds accruing to the seller.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is an assist in customs valuation?
back: Something the buyer supplies free or at reduced cost for producing the imported goods: materials or components, tools/dies/molds, merchandise consumed in production, or engineering/design work done outside the US (19 CFR 152.102).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: Which costs are excluded from US transaction value if separately identified?
back: International freight and insurance to the US; post-importation construction, assembly, maintenance or technical assistance; transportation after importation; and US duties and federal taxes owed because of importation (19 CFR 152.103).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: When can transaction value be used for a related-party purchase?
back: When the relationship did not influence the price (shown by the circumstances of sale) or the price closely approximates a test value. The importer must be able to show this.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is an ad valorem duty?
back: A duty charged as a percentage of the goods' customs value, e.g., X% of value.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What MPF do USMCA-originating goods pay on a US entry?
back: None: originating goods properly claimed under USMCA are exempt from MPF (19 CFR 24.23).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What happens to the MPF when CBP approves a US post-importation USMCA claim (19 U.S.C. 1520(d))?
back: It is refunded with the excess duty. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (Pub. L. 116-260) authorized these MPF refunds, back-dated to 1 July 2020; CBP's earlier no-refund position is superseded.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What do the HTSUS rate columns 1-General, 1-Special and 2 mean?
back: 1-General: normal trade relations (MFN) rate. 1-Special: preferential rates under trade programs and FTAs, flagged by program codes. 2: statutory rates for countries without normal trade relations.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the IGI in Mexico?
back: Impuesto General de Importación: Mexico's general import duty, with rates set by 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE and calculated mainly on customs value.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.3

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How is GST on a commercial import into Canada calculated?
back: CBSA collects it at importation on the value for tax: value for duty plus customs duties and other duties and taxes (excluding GST). GST registrants can generally claim it back as an input tax credit.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the Harmonized System (HS)?
back: The World Customs Organization's international product nomenclature: the common basis of the US, Canadian and Mexican tariffs and of most countries' trade statistics.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How is the HS organized from broadest to narrowest?
back: Sections (groups of chapters), then 2-digit chapters, 4-digit headings and 6-digit subheadings. Example: 8471.30 is chapter 84, heading 84.71, subheading 8471.30.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How often is the HS amended, and when does the next edition apply?
back: Normally about every five years. The next edition, HS 2028, takes effect 1 January 2028; every item-master classification must be checked against the correlation tables and remapped where its subheading changes.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How is a Canadian tariff classification number structured?
back: Ten digits: 6 HS digits plus 2 Canadian digits form the 8-digit tariff item, where duty rates are set; the last 2 digits are a statistical suffix.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How is a Mexican tariff classification code structured?
back: An 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE (6 HS + 2 Mexican digits; sets the duty) plus a 2-digit NICO (Número de Identificación Comercial) for commercial identification.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Sections 3.2 and 8.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 2(a) cover?
back: Incomplete or unfinished articles that have the essential character of the finished article, and complete articles presented unassembled or disassembled, are classified as the complete, finished article.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 2(b) cover?
back: A heading's reference to a material or substance includes mixtures or combinations of it with other materials. Goods of more than one material are then classified under GRI 3.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 3(a) say?
back: When goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, the heading with the most specific description is preferred over headings with a more general description.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 3(c) say?
back: When GRI 3(a) and 3(b) cannot decide, classify under the heading that occurs last in numerical order among those that equally merit consideration.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 4 say?
back: Goods that cannot be classified under GRIs 1 to 3 are classified under the heading for the goods to which they are most akin. It is rarely used.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 5 cover?
back: Containers. 5(a): specially shaped cases suitable for long-term use (e.g., camera or instrument cases) presented with their articles classify with them. 5(b): normal packing classifies with the goods unless clearly suitable for repetitive use.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What does GRI 6 say?
back: Subheadings are determined by their terms and any subheading notes, applying GRIs 1-5 by analogy and comparing only subheadings at the same level (one-dash with one-dash).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 98?
back: Special classification provisions, e.g., US goods returned (9801) or articles assembled abroad from US components (9802), which can give duty relief if their conditions and documentation requirements are met.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is CROSS?
back: CBP's Customs Rulings Online Search System (rulings.cbp.gov): a searchable database of CBP Headquarters and New York rulings from 1989 on, cross-referenced to later modifications and revocations.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is a US binding ruling?
back: A written CBP decision under 19 CFR Part 177, normally requested before import, applying the law to a specific described transaction. CBP must follow it until modified or revoked, if the facts given were accurate.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How far can we rely on a CROSS ruling issued to another importer?
back: Only as guidance. Under 19 CFR 177.9 a ruling covers the transaction it describes, and others should not assume it applies. Confirm the facts match, or request our own ruling.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What are the HS Explanatory Notes?
back: The WCO's official interpretation of the HS at the international level, describing each heading's scope, inclusions and exclusions. They are not part of the legal text; the US treats them as persuasive, not binding.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is CARM?
back: CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management: CBSA's system for assessing and collecting duties and taxes on commercial imports. It became the official system of record on 21 October 2024.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the CARM Client Portal (CCP)?
back: CBSA's online portal where importers register their business, delegate access to customs brokers, enrol in programs such as RPP, post financial security and view statements of account.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What are CBSA D-Memoranda?
back: CBSA's departmental memoranda (series D1 to D23) explaining how it applies customs legislation, regulations and policy, e.g., D10 classification, D13 valuation, D17 accounting. They are guidance, not law.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is Release Prior to Payment (RPP) in Canada?
back: A CBSA program that releases goods before duties and taxes are paid, with payment due later on the monthly statement of account. Importers must enrol and post financial security.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is Anexo 22 of Mexico's foreign-trade rules (RGCE)?
back: The instructions for completing the pedimento, including appendices (catalogues) of codes, e.g., customs offices, pedimento keys (A1 = definitive import), regimes and countries, that every pedimento must use.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the RFC?
back: Registro Federal de Contribuyentes: Mexico's federal taxpayer ID issued by SAT. The importer's RFC is declared on the pedimento and must be active to stay in the padrón de importadores.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the e.firma?
back: SAT's advanced electronic signature (formerly FIEL): personal, non-transferable credentials used to sign filings such as padrón requests, broker authorizations and electronic value declarations.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is Mexico's foreign-trade single window, and who runs it?
back: The Ventanilla Única de Trámites de Comercio Exterior (VUTCE), run by the ATDT under a decree of 4 May 2026. It replaced SAT's VUCEM, a name the trade still uses (as of Oct 2026)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the TIGIE?
back: Mexico's import and export tariff schedule, contained in the Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación (LIGIE).
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 3.2

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: When did USMCA enter into force?
back: 1 July 2020, replacing NAFTA.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is the USMCA transaction value formula for regional value content (RVC)?
back: RVC = (TV - VNM) / TV x 100, where TV is the good's transaction value adjusted to exclude international shipping costs and VNM is the value of non-originating materials.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What is accumulation under USMCA?
back: Originating materials from one USMCA country count as originating when used in another, and production by several producers across the region can be combined to meet the origin rules (Art. 4.11).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: Since when has Mexico accepted USMCA certifications completed by the importer?
back: Since 1 January 2024, after its transition period of three years and six months from entry into force.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What are the nine minimum data elements of a USMCA certification of origin?
back: 1 certifier role (importer, exporter or producer); 2 certifier; 3 exporter; 4 producer; 5 importer; 6 description and 6-digit HS classification; 7 origin criterion; 8 blanket period; 9 authorized signature and date.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: How long must customs accept a USMCA certification of origin?
back: Four years after the date it was completed (USMCA Chapter 5). This acceptance period is separate from the five-year recordkeeping requirement.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: Under USMCA Art. 34.7, what was due at the sixth-anniversary joint review (1 July 2026)?
back: The Free Trade Commission meets, and each Party confirms in writing whether it wants to extend the 16-year term for another 16 years. Outcome: docs/primers/current-tariff-landscape.md, Section 1.5 (as of Oct 2026)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Customs, classification and USMCA
front: What happens if not every USMCA Party confirms extension at the joint review?
back: The agreement stays in force; the Commission holds annual joint reviews for the rest of the term, and the Parties can still confirm extension. Without it, USMCA terminates 16 years after entry into force (2036).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'industrial' modality?
back: One company carries out an industrial process that elaborates or transforms goods for export under its own program. It is the standard modality for manufacturers.
source: Decreto IMMEX (DOF 1 Nov 2006, as amended), art. 3 (modalities)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'controladora de empresas' modality?
back: A certified controlling company integrates the manufacturing operations of one or more controlled companies under a single IMMEX program.
source: Decreto IMMEX (DOF 1 Nov 2006, as amended), art. 3 (modalities)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'servicios' modality?
back: Services performed on goods for export, or export services, limited to the activities the Secretaría de Economía lists as eligible.
source: Decreto IMMEX (DOF 1 Nov 2006, as amended), art. 3 (modalities)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'albergue' (shelter) modality?
back: One or more foreign companies supply technology and production material to a Mexican shelter company that holds the program, so they manufacture in Mexico without operating their own IMMEX program.
source: Decreto IMMEX (DOF 1 Nov 2006, as amended), art. 3 (modalities)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'terciarización' (outsourcing) modality?
back: A certified company without its own production facilities has the manufacturing done by third parties (submanufacturers) that it registers in its program (Decreto IMMEX art. 3-V).
source: Decreto IMMEX (DOF 1 Nov 2006, as amended), art. 3 (modalities)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: how long can temporarily imported machinery and equipment stay in Mexico?
back: For as long as the IMMEX program remains in force (Ley Aduanera art. 108). It can be changed to definitive import by paying the corresponding duties and taxes.
source: Ley Aduanera art. 108; Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 11.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what is a 'descargo'?
back: The discharge of a temporary-import balance, recorded when the goods, or the inputs consumed in them, leave Mexico on a return pedimento or change regime. Undischarged balances are duty and tax exposure.
source: RGCE Anexo 24; Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 11.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: why do current SAT rules call the SCCCyG annex 'Anexo 30' rather than 'Anexo 31'?
back: The annex was renumbered from 31 to 30 starting with the RGCE for 2022. Industry and some SAT pages still say 'Anexo 31'; cite it as 'Anexo 30 (formerly Anexo 31)' (as of Oct 2026)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: how do Anexo 24 and the SCCCyG depend on each other?
back: Anexo 24 tracks the physical temporary-import inventory; the SCCCyG tracks the VAT credit and guarantee accounts. Discharge reports from the Anexo 24 system feed the SCCCyG, so bad inventory data breaks both.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what does IVA/IEPS certification give a company?
back: A tax credit equal to the IVA/IEPS on its temporary imports (Ley del IVA art. 28-A, Ley del IEPS art. 15-A), so no cash VAT is paid at import.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX IMMEX: what are the VAT options for an IMMEX company without IVA/IEPS certification?
back: Pay the IVA and any IEPS on each temporary import in cash, or guarantee it with a bond (fianza) or letter of credit in favor of the treasury.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX: What is PROSEC?
back: Programas de Promoción Sectorial: a Secretaría de Economía program letting registered producers in designated sectors import listed inputs and machinery at preferential IGI rates, whether the finished goods are exported or sold in Mexico.
source: Decreto PROSEC (Programas de Promoción Sectorial), DOF 2 August 2002, as amended

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX: What is a Regla Octava (Regla 8a) permit?
back: A Secretaría de Economía prior permit, available to PROSEC producers, to import inputs under TIGIE heading 98.02 at the preferential rate, solely for producing goods of the authorized sector.
source: LIGIE article 2, complementary rule 8a (Regla Octava); Secretaría de Economía prior permit

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is 1313(a) manufacturing direct identification drawback?
back: The imported duty-paid merchandise itself is used to manufacture an article that is exported or destroyed. No substitution; use in manufacture within 5 years of import.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is 1313(c) rejected merchandise drawback?
back: Refund on imports that did not conform to sample or specifications, were defective at import, or were shipped without consent, and on retail goods returned for any reason, when exported or destroyed within 5 years of import.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is 1313(j)(1) unused merchandise direct identification drawback?
back: The same imported goods are exported or destroyed under CBP supervision within 5 years of import, without being used in the US. Operations such as repacking or testing are not 'use'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is 1313(j)(2) unused merchandise substitution drawback?
back: Refund on an import when other unused goods classifiable under the same 8-digit HTS subheading (10-digit where the 8-digit description begins 'Other') are exported or destroyed within 5 years of that import.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is TFTEA and what did it do to drawback?
back: The Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015. It modernized drawback: 8-digit HTS substitution, uniform 5-year windows and electronic filing. Claims now follow 19 CFR Part 190; legacy claims followed Part 191.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: where and how are claims filed?
back: Electronically in ACE as a drawback entry (entry type 47), with the import entries designated, proof of export or destruction, and any manufacturing records. Usually prepared by a broker or drawback specialist.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is accelerated payment?
back: A CBP privilege (19 CFR 190.92) to receive estimated drawback before the claim liquidates. Payment is not liquidation: CBP can still review the claim and recover any overpayment.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: what is a waiver of prior notice?
back: A CBP privilege (19 CFR 190.91) waiving the requirement to notify CBP before exporting or destroying goods for unused (1313(j)) or rejected (1313(c)) claims, so shipments need not wait for CBP's examination decision.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US drawback: which additional duties can never be refunded through drawback?
