back: Antidumping and countervailing duties (19 U.S.C. 1677h). For other additional duties, check the specific tariff action's terms; see docs/primers/current-tariff-landscape.md, US-10.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US: What is the Commerce Control List (CCL)?
back: Supplement No. 1 to 15 CFR Part 774: the list of items with specific EAR controls, organized into 10 categories and 5 product groups. Each entry is an ECCN with its reasons for control.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what do the first two characters of an ECCN such as 3A001 mean?
back: Digit = CCL category, 0-9 (3 = electronics). Letter = product group: A systems, equipment and components, B test and production equipment, C materials, D software, E technology.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: in an ECCN, what do the last-three-digit series 3xx and 9xx signal?
back: 3xx: chemical and biological weapons. 9xx: anti-terrorism, crime control and other controls such as UN sanctions.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: in an ECCN, what do the last-three-digit series 5xx and 6xx signal?
back: 5xx: firearms and spacecraft items, e.g., 0A501 and 9A515. 6xx: the '600 series' of military items.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: under BIS 'Know Your Customer' guidance, what must you do when a transaction shows a red flag?
back: Inquire and resolve it before proceeding; without red flags you may rely on the information received. Examples: buyer evasive about end use; product does not fit the buyer's business; a freight forwarder named as final destination.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: how do you read the Commerce Country Chart?
back: Take the reasons for control in the item's ECCN (e.g., NS1, AT1), find the destination row in Supplement No. 1 to Part 738. An X under a matching column means a license is required unless a license exception applies.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: how do OFAC and BIS differ?
back: OFAC (Treasury) administers economic sanctions on countries, regimes and listed persons, such as the SDN List, and covers transactions broadly. BIS (Commerce) controls the items exported under the EAR. A shipment may need both cleared.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what is restricted party screening?
back: Checking every party to an export (buyer, consignee, end user, agents) against government lists such as BIS's Entity List and OFAC's SDN List, typically through the Consolidated Screening List.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what is ACE AESDirect?
back: The Census Bureau's free web-based tool for filing EEI to AES, reached through an ACE exporter account. Alternatives are AESWebLink, EDI bulk upload or certified third-party software.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: when is EEI filing generally required?
back: When the value under one Schedule B/HTS number exceeds US$2,500, or at any value when a license is required or another 15 CFR 30.2(a)(1)(iv) category applies (15 CFR 30.2, 30.37(a)).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what is the ITN?
back: The Internal Transaction Number AES returns when it accepts an EEI filing. The filer gives it to the carrier as proof of filing; exempt shipments carry an exemption legend such as 'NOEEI 30.37(a)'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: who is the USPPI?
back: The US Principal Party in Interest: the person or entity in the US receiving the primary benefit, monetary or otherwise, from the export, usually the US seller or manufacturer. It answers for the EEI data it supplies.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what is a routed export transaction?
back: An export in which the foreign principal party in interest (FPPI) authorizes a US agent, often its forwarder, to file the EEI. The USPPI must still give the agent accurate data and keep records.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what are the EEI filing deadlines for vessel and air cargo (non-USML)?
back: Vessel: 24 hours before loading at the US port. Air: 2 hours before scheduled departure (15 CFR 30.4(b)).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: what are the EEI filing deadlines for truck and rail cargo (non-USML)?
back: Truck: 1 hour before the truck arrives at the US border. Rail: 2 hours before the train arrives at the border (15 CFR 30.4(b)).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: US export: how long must EEI-supporting records be kept?
back: Five years from the date of export (15 CFR 30.10), by the USPPI, the authorized agent and other parties to the transaction.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: CA: What is CERS?
back: The Canada Border Services Agency's Canadian Export Reporting System: a free online portal exporters use to file Canadian export declarations. It replaced paper B13A reporting.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: CA: When must a commercial export from Canada be reported to the CBSA?
back: Generally when going to a country other than the US, Puerto Rico or the US Virgin Islands with a value of CAD 2,000 or more, or when the goods are controlled, regulated or prohibited (Memorandum D20-1-1).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: CA: What export reporting do most Canadian exports to the US need?
back: None: goods exported for consumption in the US generally need no export declaration; controlled goods present their permit instead. Goods transiting the US to a third country must be reported.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: MX: What is an export pedimento?
back: The customs declaration an agente aduanal files to export goods from Mexico. For IMMEX companies, the return pedimento is the evidence that discharges temporary imports in Anexo 24 and the SCCCyG.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: what is a cost roll (rollup)?
back: Calculating each item's total standard by summing its cost elements, and for kits or assemblies its components' costs, into a pending cost that is reviewed before it is posted.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: what is the difference between a pending and a frozen cost?
back: Pending: a proposed cost from a cost roll that does not yet value anything. Frozen: the current standard used for transactions. Oracle EBS (our ERP) uses these names.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: what happens to on-hand inventory when a standard cost update posts?
back: It is revalued: on-hand (and in-transit) quantity x (new standard - old standard) is booked to a revaluation account. A big duty change on a high-stock item makes a big adjustment.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: 1,000 units on hand; the standard rises from $12.00 to $12.90 for higher duty. What is the revaluation?
back: 1,000 x ($12.90 - $12.00) = $900 increase in inventory value, posted to the revaluation account. Finance should get this estimate before approving the update.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: what is the trade-off in how often standards are updated?
back: Frequent updates keep standards close to actual (smaller PPV, truer margins) but add workload, revaluation noise and control risk. Infrequent updates are stable but let variances grow when duty or freight move.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: before approving a cost update, which two completeness checks does the reviewer run?
back: Reconcile item counts and totals to the source extract, and check for zero, blank and new-item costs.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: before approving a cost update, which two reasonableness checks does the reviewer run?
back: Review the largest percent and dollar changes (top movers), and compare the inventory revaluation estimate with Finance's expectation.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: under the usual sign convention, what does a positive PPV mean?
back: Unfavorable: we paid more than standard. A negative PPV is favorable. Confirm how our reports sign it [COMPANY: PPV sign convention], because some reports flip the sign.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Standard cost: standard $10.00, PO price $10.40, 500 units received. What is the PPV?
back: (10.40 - 10.00) x 500 = $200 unfavorable (positive PPV): we paid $200 more than standard for this receipt.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Landed cost (US): FOB price $10,000, ocean freight $1,200, duty 25% ad valorem. What are the duty and landed cost before fees?
back: Duty = 25% x $10,000 = $2,500, because international freight is excluded from US customs value. Landed cost before fees = $10,000 + $1,200 + $2,500 = $13,700.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.7

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Landed cost (MX): price $10,000, freight to the border $1,200, IGI 25%. What is the IGI?
back: 25% x $11,200 = $2,800, because Mexico's customs value includes freight and insurance to the point of entry. DTA and IVA come on top of this.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Sections 6.3 and 9.3

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Landed cost: how should freight be allocated to items?
back: By a documented driver that matches what drives the cost, such as weight or cubic volume, applied consistently. The choice shifts cost between heavy, cheap items and light, expensive ones.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Landed cost: why can't a cost model use only the HTS base (column 1) duty rate?
back: Additional Chapter 99 duties, USMCA preference, exclusions and AD/CVD can change the effective rate. Research's Tariff-Impact Brief supplies the applicable rate stack per item and origin.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms: what are the Incoterms 2020 rules?
back: The ICC's 11 standard trade terms, in effect since 1 January 2020. They allocate delivery, risk transfer, carriage, insurance and export/import clearance between seller and buyer. They do not set price or title transfer.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under EXW, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The buyer pays everything from the seller's premises: loading, export clearance, main carriage, insurance, import clearance and duties. The seller only makes the goods available.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under FCA, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The buyer. The seller clears export and hands the goods to the buyer's carrier at the named place, where risk passes. FCA suits any transport mode, including containers.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under FOB, who pays ocean freight and import duty?
back: The buyer. The seller clears export and loads the goods on board at the named port of shipment, where risk passes. FOB is for sea and inland waterway transport only.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, who pays ocean freight, insurance and import duty?
back: Seller pays ocean freight and insurance to the destination port; buyer pays import clearance and duty. Sea and inland waterway only.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, what minimum insurance cover must the seller buy?
back: Minimum cover under Institute Cargo Clauses (C), unless the parties agree otherwise. CIP, by contrast, requires broader Clauses (A) cover.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, where does risk pass from seller to buyer?
back: When the goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment, even though the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under DAP, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The seller pays carriage and bears risk to the named destination, goods ready for unloading. The buyer unloads, clears import and pays duties and taxes.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: under DDP, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The seller pays everything to the named destination, including import clearance, duties and taxes. Risky where a foreign seller cannot act as importer.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms 2020: why does ICC advise FCA instead of FOB for container shipments?
back: Under FOB, risk passes only when goods are on board, but the seller loses control of a container at the terminal before loading. FCA passes risk at handover to the carrier.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms: why do they matter for landed and standard cost data?
back: They show which costs are already in the supplier price (freight under CIF or DAP) and which we add (freight under FOB or FCA; duty unless DDP), avoiding double counts or gaps.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.6

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Incoterms (US): if we buy CIF, why isn't the CIF price our US customs value?
back: US transaction value excludes international freight and insurance. A CIF price includes them, so the identified freight and insurance are deducted. FOB and FCA prices normally exclude them already.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.3

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Tariff action (US): how is a new additional duty built into the HTSUS?
back: Through new Chapter 99 headings and US notes listing covered HTS codes, rates and exceptions. The entry reports the Chapter 99 number together with the Chapter 1-97 classification.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Tariff action (US): why can a new duty hit goods already sitting in a US bonded warehouse?
back: Warehoused goods pay the rate in effect when they are withdrawn for consumption, not when they entered the warehouse (19 CFR 141.69).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Tariff action (US): what is an in-transit provision?
back: An exception for goods already loaded and in transit on the final mode of transport before the effective time, if entered by a stated later deadline. Terms differ by action and are claimed with a specific Chapter 99 number.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Tariff action (US): what is a product exclusion?
back: A product-specific carve-out from an additional duty, granted through a process defined by that action (e.g., USTR exclusions under Section 301). It has an exact description, dates and its own Chapter 99 number.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::Programs, exports and cost
front: Tariff action (US): why can't you model a new additional duty from the HTS code alone?
back: Applicability can also depend on country of origin, USMCA status, metal or other content, exclusions and entry date. The model needs those attributes for each item.
source: Current Tariff Landscape, Section 2.5 (checks 4 to 7 and 16)

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Requirement vs specification: what is the difference?
back: A requirement states what the business needs and why, without choosing a solution. A specification states how the solution meets it: fields, rules, screens, interfaces. The business approves requirements; the build team works from specifications.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What does MoSCoW stand for in prioritization?
back: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time). Won't-haves are agreed out of scope for now, which is what stops scope creep.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is an acceptance criterion?
back: A specific, testable pass/fail condition a requirement or story must meet before the business accepts it. Write it before the build starts so the tester and the developer read the same target.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is the user story format?
back: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit], plus acceptance criteria. Example: As a Research BSA, I want rates effective-dated, so that entries before a change keep the old rate.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What do the letters in RACI mean?
back: Responsible: does the work. Accountable: the one person who signs off. Consulted: gives input before (two-way). Informed: told after (one-way). Each task has exactly one A.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is a Definition of Ready?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet before work starts, for example: acceptance criteria written, data sources and dependencies known, and sized at 5 working days or less (otherwise split).
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is a Definition of Done?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet to count as finished, for example: tested against its acceptance criteria, reviewed by a second person (maker-checker), and accepted by the business owner.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is change control?
back: The process that puts every change to a system or agreed scope through assessment (impact, risk, effort) and approval before it is made, with a record, so nothing reaches production unreviewed.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is UAT (user acceptance testing)?
back: Business users confirm the system supports their real processes with realistic data before go-live. It answers 'can we run the business on it?', not 'does the code work?'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: UAT entry criteria: which earlier testing must be complete before UAT starts?
back: System and integration testing passed, with no open critical defects. UAT tests business fit, not whether the code works.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: UAT entry criteria: besides passed system testing, what must be ready before UAT starts?
back: The build deployed to the UAT environment, test data loaded, and approved test cases with testers available.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: UAT exit criteria: what formally closes UAT?
back: Documented sign-off by the business owner, given after the test and defect criteria are met.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Defect severity vs priority?
back: Severity is the impact on the business or system. Priority is how soon it must be fixed. A wrong label on a management report can be low severity but high priority before a board meeting.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Positive test vs negative test?
back: A positive test uses valid input and expects success. A negative test uses invalid or edge input (blank HTS, end date before start date, duplicate line) and expects a controlled rejection or error message.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is a data mapping specification?
back: A document that maps each target field to its source field or fields, with the rule that transforms it, its validation and its owner. Conversion, interfaces and their tests are built from it.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Data mapping: what is a transformation rule?
back: The logic between source and target, such as a lookup, a default or a reformat. Write it so developer and tester read it the same way, e.g. 'remove dots from the HTS; keep as 10-character text'.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is a system of record?
back: The authoritative source for a data element; every other system reads from it or syncs to it. Ask it for each field you map, e.g. is item origin mastered in Oracle or in the trade system?

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is cutover?
back: The planned, time-boxed switch from the old system to the new: final conversion, validation, then a go/no-go decision. It needs a tested rollback plan.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 6.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is hypercare?
back: A defined period right after go-live with extra support: fast defect triage, daily checks of key outputs and quick fixes, before normal support takes over.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 6.1

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?
back: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match. Use LEFT to keep, and count, orphans.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: WHERE vs HAVING?
back: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test COUNT or SUM. Example: GROUP BY entry_no, line_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 finds duplicate keys.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: why can a column alias made in SELECT be used in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?
back: Logical processing order: FROM and WHERE run before SELECT, and ORDER BY runs after it. So the alias does not exist yet when WHERE is evaluated.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: the GROUP BY rule for the SELECT list?
back: Every selected column that is not inside an aggregate (SUM, COUNT...) must be in GROUP BY. You get one output row per distinct combination of the GROUP BY columns.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: what does a comparison with NULL return?
back: UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, because NULL means the value is unknown. So column = NULL never matches. Test with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: why does WHERE program_claimed <> 'USMCA' skip lines with no program?
back: For a NULL program_claimed the comparison returns UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Write WHERE program_claimed IS NULL, or add OR program_claimed IS NULL.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
back: COUNT(*) counts rows, NULLs and duplicates included. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. So COUNT(*) - COUNT(column) is the number of NULLs in that column.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: what does COALESCE do?
back: Returns the first argument that is not NULL. COALESCE(LEFT(hts10, 2), 'UNK') labels lines with a missing HTS instead of letting them drop out of a report.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: what is a CTE?
back: A common table expression: a temporary named result set defined with WITH and used in one statement. It turns a long query into named steps you can check one at a time.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: what is a window function?
back: A function computed over a set of rows related to the current row, defined by OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). Unlike GROUP BY it keeps every row. Used for ranks, running totals, de-duplication.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: how do you keep one row per key when a file was loaded twice?
back: Number the copies with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY the key columns ORDER BY ...) and keep the rows where the number is 1. Then check: clean rows = distinct keys.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: how do you pick the rate in effect on the entry date?
back: Join on the keys AND entry_date BETWEEN effective_from AND effective_to. Then prove exactly one match per line: row count after the join equals row count before.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: T-SQL: what does 12 / 9 return?
back: 1. Integer divided by integer truncates. Annualize with SUM(x) * 12.0 / 9 so it also works on INT columns such as qty; never SUM(x) * (12 / 9).

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: SQL: why store money as DECIMAL, not FLOAT?
back: FLOAT is an approximate binary type, so sums can drift by fractions of a cent and fail to tie out. DECIMAL(p,s) stores exact decimal values.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: What is a star schema?
back: A fact table in the center joined by keys to dimension tables, with dimensions not chained to each other. Simple to query, and the shape Power BI models work best with.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Slowly changing dimension: Type 1 vs Type 2?
back: Type 1 overwrites the old value, so history is lost. Type 2 adds a new row with valid-from and valid-to dates, so old facts keep the value in effect then, such as an item's HTS before a reclassification.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Power Query vs DAX: which does what?
back: Power Query (M) imports and shapes data before it reaches the model: clean, merge, set types. DAX calculates on the loaded model: measures and calculated columns. Clean in Power Query, calculate in DAX.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Power BI: calculated column vs measure?
back: A calculated column is computed per row at refresh and stored: use it for attributes you slice by. A measure is computed when queried, in the current filter context: use it for totals and ratios.

deck: BSA Onboarding::Reference (browse only)::BSA craft and data
front: Power BI: what is filter context?
back: The set of filters in force when a measure is evaluated: from slicers, from the visual itself, and from page or report filters, spread through relationships. Same measure, different context, different value.
